cards.question: How did Arthur Samuel (1959) define machine learning?
cards.answer: The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.
distractors: The study of whether a machine can imitate a human well enough to be mistaken for one.
The design of search and pathfinding algorithms that rely on explicit knowledge representations.
The field of storing and querying large collections of data in database systems.

cards.question: According to Tom Mitchell's definition of a well-posed learning problem, when is a computer program said to learn?
cards.answer: When its performance at a class of tasks T, as measured by a performance measure P, improves with experience E.
distractors: When it can imitate a human so that an observer cannot tell them apart.
When it has been explicitly programmed with a rule for every task in T.
When it reaches zero error on the examples it has already seen in E.

cards.question: In Mitchell's framework applied to Samuel's checkers program, what plays the role of the performance measure P?
cards.answer: Whether the program wins or loses a game.
distractors: Playing 10,000 games against itself.
The task of playing checkers.
The learned value of each board position.

cards.question: In Mitchell's framework applied to Samuel's checkers program, what is the experience E?
cards.answer: Playing 10,000 games against itself.
distractors: Winning or losing a game.
The class of tasks of playing checkers.
Being explicitly programmed with expert checkers rules.

cards.question: Why did Alan Turing propose replacing the question 'Can a machine think?' with the imitation game?
cards.answer: Because the terms 'machine' and 'think' are undefined, so he instead asked whether a machine can imitate a human.
distractors: Because universal computing had already proven that machines cannot think.
Because thinking can only be defined through a performance measure P on tasks T.
Because a checkers program had already shown that machines learn like children.

cards.question: What characterises machine learning as a field distinct from other areas of AI?
cards.answer: It focuses on general learning algorithms that improve gradually with training time and data, and de-emphasises explicit knowledge representations.
distractors: It focuses on search and pathfinding algorithms rather than learning.
It relies on explicit, hand-crafted knowledge representations for each problem.
It develops a specialised algorithm for each individual task instead of general ones.

cards.question: Of the reasons given for why machine learning has advanced so much recently, which is the technological reason?
cards.answer: Faster computers, especially graphics processing units (GPUs).
distractors: Increased availability of large, good datasets.
Libraries that automate routine tasks and increased sharing of code.
Greatly increased resource allocation.

cards.question: In the plot of error against training set size, how does a very flexible model compare with a not-so-flexible model?
cards.answer: The very flexible model has higher error on small training sets but reaches much lower error as the training set grows.
distractors: The very flexible model has lower error at every training set size.
The very flexible model is better on small training sets but levels off at a higher error on large ones.
Both models converge to the same error once the training set is large enough.

cards.question: On the model-complexity spectrum, in which direction do regularization and bagging/boosting move a model?
cards.answer: Regularization moves a model toward less complexity, while bagging/boosting moves it toward more complexity.
distractors: Regularization increases complexity, while bagging/boosting reduces it.
Both regularization and bagging/boosting increase model complexity.
Both regularization and bagging/boosting reduce model complexity.

cards.question: Which of these models lies at the least complex end of the model-complexity spectrum?
cards.answer: Linear/logistic regression.
distractors: Decision tree.
Random forest.
Small neural network.

cards.question: In the data-modelling pipeline, which stage includes feature extraction, similarity measures, summary statistics and data visualization?
cards.answer: Data preparation.
distractors: Data modelling.
Evaluation.
Result dissemination.

cards.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning tasks?
cards.answer: Supervised tasks are predictive and use some variables to predict another variable; unsupervised tasks are descriptive and find human-interpretable patterns in the data.
distractors: Supervised tasks are descriptive and find patterns; unsupervised tasks are predictive.
Supervised tasks always produce continuous outputs; unsupervised tasks always produce discrete outputs.
Supervised tasks need a similarity measure between objects; unsupervised tasks need class labels.

cards.question: What is the key difference between classification and regression?
cards.answer: Classification predicts a discrete output (a class label); regression predicts a continuous output value.
distractors: Classification predicts a continuous value; regression predicts a class label.
Classification is unsupervised; regression is supervised.
Classification groups objects by similarity without labels; regression detects abnormal objects.

cards.question: Predicting wind velocity as a function of temperature, humidity and air pressure is an example of which task?
cards.answer: Regression, because the output is a continuous value.
distractors: Classification, because the inputs are measured attributes.
Clustering, because the weather variables form natural groups.
Representation learning, because wind velocity is a latent factor.

cards.question: Recognising dubious credit card transactions based on the card holder's transaction history is an example of which task?
cards.answer: Anomaly detection.
distractors: Clustering.
Regression.
Representation learning.

cards.question: Grouping documents by their word frequencies so that a search can return related documents that lack the exact keywords is which task?
cards.answer: Clustering.
distractors: Regression.
Anomaly detection.
Classification.

cards.question: Besides the features of each object, what must be defined before clustering can be performed?
cards.answer: A measure of similarity between objects.
distractors: A class label for each object.
A continuous target variable for each object.
A performance measure P based on wins and losses.

cards.question: In representation learning, what does the encoder Enc: R^D → R^d do?
cards.answer: It maps each data point to a d-dimensional latent representation that captures the latent factors describing the data.
distractors: It maps latent representations back into reconstructions in the original D-dimensional space.
It assigns each data point a discrete class label.
It removes outliers from the data before modelling.

cards.question: Which machine learning task is described as the foundation of generative AI such as image/video generation and LLMs?
cards.answer: Representation learning.
distractors: Clustering.
Anomaly detection.
Regression.

cards.question: What is the generalization error of a learned prediction rule f?
cards.answer: How often f makes a mistake on future, previously unseen data.
distractors: How often f makes a mistake on the training data it was learned from.
The difference between the number of training and test objects.
The error introduced by noise in the training set measurements.

cards.question: Points with −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 and y ≤ 1 are blue, all others red. With z1 = max{0, x−1} + max{0, −1−x} and z2 = max{0, −1+y}, which decision rule solves the problem?
cards.answer: Classify as blue if z1 = z2 = 0, otherwise red.
distractors: Classify as blue if z1 = z2 = 1, otherwise red.
Classify as blue if z1 = 1 and z2 = 0, otherwise red.
Classify as blue if z1 = 0 and z2 = 1, otherwise red.

cards.question: A decision rule built from terms like max{0, x−1} and max{0, −1+y} is a slightly obscured example of which model?
cards.answer: A neural network with ReLU units.
distractors: A decision tree.
A K-nearest neighbour classifier.
A linear regression model.

cards.question: Relative CO2 concentration oscillates with a period of one year while trending upward over time. Which function is a good candidate model y = f(x), with x in years?
cards.answer: y = 0.5x + sin(2πx).
distractors: y = 0.5x + cos(x).
y = −0.5x + sin(2πx).
y = −0.5x + cos(x).

cards.question: Extending f(x; w) = w0 + w1x1 + w2x2 with the terms w3x1² + w4x2² is an example of what?
cards.answer: A polynomial feature transformation, also called basis expansion.
distractors: Standardization of the input attributes.
One-out-of-K encoding of the inputs.
Dimensionality reduction of the inputs.

cards.question: In a data table, a collection of attributes describing a single object (a row) is also known as what?
cards.answer: A record, point, case, sample, entity or instance.
distractors: A variable, feature or characteristic.
A class label.
A latent factor.

cards.question: Which of these attributes is discrete rather than continuous?
cards.answer: Zip codes.
distractors: Temperature.
Height.
Weight.

cards.question: Which operations are meaningful for a nominal attribute such as eye colour?
cards.answer: Only equal / not equal.
distractors: Greater than / less than.
Addition / subtraction.
Multiplication / division.

cards.question: What distinguishes a ratio attribute from an interval attribute?
cards.answer: For a ratio attribute, zero means absence of what is measured, so multiplication and division are meaningful.
distractors: A ratio attribute can be ranked, whereas an interval attribute cannot.
An interval attribute is always continuous, while a ratio attribute is always discrete.
An interval attribute supports multiplication and division, while a ratio attribute only supports addition and subtraction.

cards.question: How is temperature classified in Celsius versus in Kelvin?
cards.answer: Interval in Celsius, ratio in Kelvin.
distractors: Ratio in both Celsius and Kelvin.
Ratio in Celsius, interval in Kelvin.
Ordinal in Celsius, ratio in Kelvin.

cards.question: How should military rank be classified?
cards.answer: Discrete and ordinal.
distractors: Discrete and nominal.
Continuous and interval.
Discrete and ratio.

cards.question: Why is a person's year of birth classified as interval while their age in years is ratio?
cards.answer: For age, zero means absence of what is measured, so ratios are meaningful; year zero does not mean absence of anything, so only differences between years are meaningful.
distractors: Year of birth is continuous while age in years is discrete.
Age can be ranked but year of birth cannot.
Year of birth is only a category label, so it supports equality comparisons alone.

cards.question: From your own perspective as a customer, how is a coat check number classified?
cards.answer: Discrete and nominal.
distractors: Discrete and ordinal.
Discrete and ratio.
Continuous and interval.

cards.question: In a cereal dataset, TYPE (0 = served cold, 1 = served hot) and VIT (0%, 25% or 100% of recommendations) are both discrete. How do they differ?
cards.answer: TYPE is nominal because hot is not greater than cold, while VIT is ordinal because 0% < 25% < 100%.
distractors: Both are ordinal, because both are coded with numbers.
TYPE is ordinal and VIT is nominal.
TYPE is ratio because 0 means absence of heat, while VIT is interval.

cards.question: Which operations can be applied to a ratio attribute?
cards.answer: All of =, ≠, <, >, +, −, × and /, because a ratio attribute is also interval, ordinal and nominal.
distractors: Only × and /.
Only =, ≠, < and >.
Only +, −, × and /, but not equality comparisons.

cards.question: A dataset recording which people know each other is best described as which data set type and representation?
cards.answer: Relational data, represented as a graph (or an adjacency matrix).
distractors: Record/tabular data, represented as a transaction table.
Ordered data, represented as a sequence.
Sequential data, represented as a time series.

cards.question: How is market basket transaction data turned into a matrix?
cards.answer: One row per transaction and one binary column per item, with a 1 if the item was bought in that transaction.
distractors: One row and one column per item, with a 1 if two items were ever bought together.
One row per time step and one column holding the number of items bought.
One column per transaction, holding the list of item names.

cards.question: When is data considered to be of high quality?
cards.answer: When it is fit for its intended purpose and correctly represents the phenomena it corresponds to.
distractors: When it contains no missing values, regardless of its purpose.
When all its attributes have been standardized.
When it contains as many attributes as possible.

cards.question: What is the difference between noise and outliers?
cards.answer: Noise is an unwanted perturbation to a signal, while an outlier is a data object significantly different from most others, which can even be a natural property of the data.
distractors: Noise is a data object significantly different from the others, while an outlier is a perturbation to a signal.
Both are always caused by measurement error and must always be removed.
Outliers are missing values encoded with a special placeholder value.

cards.question: Which of these is a cause of noise in data?
cards.answer: Interference from other signals or limits in measurement accuracy.
distractors: An attribute that is not applicable to the object.
People declining to give information.
A data object being a natural extreme of the population.

cards.question: Annual income being recorded as missing for a child is an example of which cause of missing values?
cards.answer: The attribute is not applicable to that object.
distractors: The information was not collected because the person declined to give it.
Noise from limits in measurement accuracy.
An outlier caused by a measurement error.

cards.question: Replacing a missing age with the average age of the other data objects is which strategy for handling missing values?
cards.answer: Estimating the missing values.
distractors: Removing data objects.
Eliminating attributes.
Ignoring the missing value in the analysis.

cards.question: What is the difference between feature subset selection and feature extraction?
cards.answer: Feature subset selection keeps a subset of the existing attributes, while feature extraction creates new features from existing ones.
distractors: Feature subset selection creates new features, while feature extraction keeps a subset of existing ones.
Feature subset selection picks a representative subset of data objects, while feature extraction picks attributes.
Both project the data onto a low-dimensional subspace.

cards.question: Which dataset manipulation projects the data onto a low-dimensional subspace?
cards.answer: Dimensionality reduction.
distractors: Sampling.
Discretization and binarization.
Aggregation of several attributes into one.

cards.question: When is de-trending an appropriate feature processing step?
cards.answer: When the data is not stationary, such as a signal with an underlying trend.
distractors: When text documents contain many common stop words.
When categorical attributes need to become binary columns.
When images need to be centered, rotated and scaled.

cards.question: How is an attribute standardized?
cards.answer: Subtract the attribute's estimated mean and divide by its estimated standard deviation.
distractors: Set each value to 1 if it is at least a threshold θ, otherwise 0.
Divide each value by the attribute's maximum value.
Replace each value with a binary indicator vector over its categories.

cards.question: What does binarizing an attribute with threshold θ produce?
cards.answer: A value of 1 if x ≥ θ and 0 otherwise.
distractors: A value of (x − mean) / standard deviation.
One binary column per category of the attribute.
A value of 1 if x is missing and 0 otherwise.

cards.question: A Nationality attribute takes the values Denmark, Norway and Sweden. What does one-out-of-K encoding do with it?
cards.answer: It replaces it with three binary columns, one per country, where exactly one column is 1 for each object.
distractors: It replaces each country with a single integer code 1, 2 or 3.
It standardizes the column to zero mean and unit variance.
It removes the attribute because it is not numeric.

cards.question: What information does a bag-of-words representation of a text discard?
cards.answer: Grammar and word order, since the text is treated as an unordered collection of words.
distractors: Which words occur in the text.
How many times each word occurs.
Which document each word belongs to.

cards.question: Removing words such as 'the', 'is' and 'of' before building a bag-of-words matrix is called what?
cards.answer: Elimination of stop words.
distractors: Stemming.
De-trending.
One-out-of-K encoding.

cards.question: In a bag-of-words matrix, 'words' and 'word' are merged into a single entry with count 2. Which processing step caused this?
cards.answer: Stemming, which reduces word variants to a common stem.
distractors: Stop word elimination.
Binarization of word counts.
Sampling of sentences.

cards.question: A dataset of N handwritten digit images, each 28 × 28 pixels, is vectorized into a data matrix X. What is the shape of X?
What are the two main purposes of visualizing data?
cards.answer: Exploratory data analysis to detect new patterns, and disseminating results in written work.
distractors: Removing noise and filling in missing values.
Training models and computing their generalization error.
Encoding categorical attributes and reducing dimensionality.

cards.question: Why is a bar chart usually better than a pie chart for comparing three similar proportions?
cards.answer: Differences in bar height are easier to judge than differences in area.
distractors: Pie charts cannot show more than two categories.
Bar charts automatically standardize the data.
Area is easier to compare than height, so the pie hides the categories.

cards.question: Choosing the viewpoint, transparency, separation and grouping of visual elements belongs to which visualization decision?
cards.answer: Arrangement.
distractors: Representation.
Selection.
Necessity.

cards.question: A plot cannot clearly show every data object in a huge dataset. Which is a selection technique for reducing the number of objects shown?
cards.answer: Random sampling, displaying a region of interest, or using density estimation.
distractors: Plotting pairs of attributes.
Switching to a 3D scatter plot.
Applying one-out-of-K encoding.

cards.question: What determines the shape of a histogram?
cards.answer: The distribution of the data and the number of bins (bin width).
distractors: Only the distribution of the data.
The ordering of the attributes.
The mean and standard deviation alone.

cards.question: In a box plot, what do the edges of the box and the line inside it represent?
cards.answer: The box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles, and the line marks the median.
distractors: The box spans the mean ± one standard deviation, and the line marks the mean.
The box spans the minimum to maximum, and the line marks the mean.
The box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles, and the line marks the mean.

cards.question: Where does the upper whisker of a box plot end?
cards.answer: At min(max(data), q75 + 1.5(q75 − q25)), the most extreme value that is not an outlier.
distractors: Always at q75 + 1.5(q75 − q25), even beyond the data.
Always at the maximum of the data.

cards.question: Two standardized attributes have box plots with very similar shapes. Can you conclude that they are correlated?
cards.answer: No. Correlation depends on whether they take high or low values together, which a box plot cannot show.
distractors: Yes, similar distributions imply strong positive correlation.
Yes, as long as both attributes have outliers on the same side.
No, because standardized attributes can never be correlated.

cards.question: A standardized attribute shows a squashed box near zero and many extreme values far above it. Is it likely to be normally distributed?
cards.answer: No. It is highly right-skewed rather than symmetric.
distractors: Yes, because standardization makes any attribute normal.
Yes, because the median is close to zero.
No, because it must be a discrete nominal attribute.

cards.question: A binary gender attribute (0 = female, 1 = male) shows a single extreme value marker below a collapsed box. How should this be interpreted?
cards.answer: It is not a real outlier. The marker corresponds to the females, and it shows that more than 75% of observations are male.
distractors: It is a clear outlier that should be removed.
It shows a recording error in the gender attribute.
It shows that more than 75% of observations are female.

cards.question: What are scatter plots mainly used for?
cards.answer: Showing relations between attributes, assessing their dependence, and, with classes, assessing separability.
distractors: Showing the distribution of a single attribute using bins.
Showing each object as a line across parallel axes.
Showing percentiles and extreme values of one attribute.

cards.question: What is the recommended stance on 3D scatter plots?
cards.answer: They are often confusing and should be avoided if possible.
distractors: They should always be preferred because they show more attributes.
They are required whenever the data has more than two classes.
They are the best way to show the distribution of a single attribute.

cards.question: What does a scatter plot matrix display?
cards.answer: Scatter plots of all pairs of attributes.
distractors: The similarity between every pair of objects.
Each object as a line connecting its values on parallel axes.
The raw normalized data matrix as a grey-scale image.

cards.question: In a parallel coordinates plot, how is each data object represented, and why does attribute order matter?
cards.answer: Each object is a line connecting its values on parallel axes, and the attribute order affects whether groups of similar lines become visible.
distractors: Each object is a point on perpendicular axes, and order only affects the axis labels.
Each attribute is a line, and order determines the class labels.
Each object is a bar, and order determines the bin width.

cards.question: When is a plot of the raw data matrix most useful?
cards.answer: When the objects are sorted by class, typically with normalized attributes.
distractors: When the objects are in random order and the attributes are unnormalized.
When there is only one attribute to show.
When the goal is to show the relation between a pair of objects only.

cards.question: Which ACCENT principle asks whether the most important elements of a graph are also the most visually prominent?
cards.answer: Clarity.
distractors: Apprehension.
Efficiency.
Necessity.

cards.question: Which ACCENT principle asks whether you have used the same colours, shapes, etc. as in your other graphs?
cards.answer: Consistency.
distractors: Clarity.
Truthfulness.
Apprehension.

cards.question: What does Tufte's data-ink ratio measure, and what should you do with it?
cards.answer: It is the data-ink divided by the total ink used, and it should be maximized.
distractors: It is the total ink divided by the data-ink, and it should be maximized.
It is the number of data points divided by the plot area, and it should be minimized.
It is the data-ink divided by the total ink used, and it should be minimized.

cards.question: When treating a figure like technical writing, how many questions or points should a single figure address, and what makes it stand-alone?
cards.answer: A single question or point per figure, made stand-alone through labels, titles and captions.
distractors: As many points as possible per figure, to save space in the text.
A single point per figure, explained only in the main text with no labels.
Several related points per figure, distinguished only by colour.

cards.question: What does the Iris dataset contain?
cards.answer: 150 flowers, 50 from each of three Iris classes, described by sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width.
distractors: 150 flowers from five classes, described by petal attributes only.
50 flowers in total from three classes, described by four attributes.
150 flowers from three classes, described by colour and height.

cards.question: In 02452, how many of the 12 assignments must be approved to be able to pass the course?
cards.answer: 8 out of 12.
distractors: 6 out of 12.
10 out of 12.
All 12.
